title: Why do we hate?
hookLine: Sakka, king of the gods, asks why beings who wish to live without hate still live in hate
last: IT WAS GRAND ONCE, AND IT'S GONE.

lines: A LOVE SONG OUTSIDE A CAVE.
THE STRINGS AND VOICE BLEND WELL.
THE KING OF THE GODS ASKS.
cards: Before the question, a love song. Sakka, king of the gods, wants to see the Buddha, who is sitting in a cave in the hills near Rajagaha. He doesn't just walk in.
He sends ahead a celestial musician, Pancasikha, with a lute. Pancasikha stands near the cave and sings a song that mixes praise of the Buddha with longing for a girl he loves.
The Buddha listens, and then tells him, kindly: the strings and your voice blend well. Then Sakka comes in, and asks his question.

teach.b: The Sakkapanha, Sakka's questions, is the twenty-first Long Discourse. The first question goes like this.
Gods, humans, and every other kind of being all wish to live without hate, without violence, without enemies, without ill will. And yet they live in hate, with violence, with enemies. Why?
Look at the shape of it. Not, why are other people hateful? Everyone wants peace.
Everyone ends up in conflict anyway. What's tying them?
The Buddha answers: envy and stinginess. Envy, at what someone else has. Stinginess, about what you have.
Sakka is pleased, and asks the obvious next question: and where do those come from?
From what we hold dear and what we don't. And that? From desire, wanting.
And desire? From thinking, the mind turning something over. And thinking?

From what the sutta calls the spreading of perception: the mind taking one small thing and running with it, building a story, then another story on top. Each answer goes one layer down, like peeling a root.
And it ends somewhere surprisingly ordinary.
In this answer, hate between nations and hate between neighbors start in the same place: a mind that proliferates.
Read that way, the answer is both bleak and hopeful. Bleak, because the root is in every mind. Hopeful, because it sits in a place anyone can watch.
Sakka says, as each answer lands: so it is, Blessed One. My doubt is cut off.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the chain in Sakka's questions to show how conflict starts in the mind, and in Theravada countries Sakka is a familiar figure in temple art and stories as a devoted protector of the teaching.

o: anger and fear, the roots of every war
envy and stinginess, binding beings to hate
pride and greed, the faults of kings

games.q: why do we hate?: tap the pairs.
p: king of the gods, who asks

s: Sakka asks why other beings are so hateful
he asks why all beings, who wish to live without hate, still live in it.
the Buddha's first answer is envy and stinginess
then he traces them back, layer by layer.
the Buddha scolds Pancasikha for singing a love song
he says the strings and the voice blend well.

games.q: you're Sakka. the Buddha has said beings live in hate because of envy and stinginess. what do you ask next?
o: where envy and stinginess come from.
whether the gods are free of them.
games.why: he asks for the source, again and again, until the answer reaches the spreading of perception in the mind.

practice: Ask one honest question about yourself, not about anyone else: who do I resent right now, and what do I want that they have? Or: what am I holding tightly?
Ask it, breathe, and see if the answer goes one layer deeper on its own; if the mind starts building a story, notice the building.

wordCard.voice: Issa-macchariya. Sakka's first question in DN 21; the Buddha answers envy and stinginess, rooted in what we hold dear, desire, and the spreading mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali issa-macchariya: envy and stinginess, the fetters the Buddha names for Sakka.

carryVoice: Your line: one layer down. Envy and stinginess, and under them, a mind that spreads. Go gently.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 21 (Sakkapanha Sutta), Pancasikha's song and Sakka's first questions
